extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for evaluating inductive reasoning and the establishment of laws of nature: when an induction is warranted, how inductions interrelate, and what experimental and deductive supports are required. Emphasises distinction between simple enumeration and more rigorous inductive methods, the role of prior generalizations, and the parsimony/simplicity of laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of the universal major (uniformity axiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal major premiss of inductive syllogisms (that nature is governed by general laws) must be justified; it is not self-evident and cannot be assumed without argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asks 'Whence came the universal major? What proves to us that nature is governed by general laws?' and stresses that the principle of the uniformity of the course of nature must be examined and its terms strictly explained before admitting its truth. One must not take this axiom for granted when constructing inductive proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on simple enumeration (inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by mere enumeration — concluding a general truth because no contrary instance has been observed — is an insufficient method for scientific inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon's condemned 'Inductio per enumerationem simplicem' is described as natural to uncultivated minds and adequate only provisionally; science requires seeking conflicting instances, experimenting, and 'interrogating nature' rather than passively accepting observed coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of assurance that counterinstances would have been observed
rubrics_metrics.description: Before concluding universality from absence of counterexamples, it must be proved that if counterinstances existed we would have known of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states: 'Before we can be at liberty to conclude that something is universally true because we have never known an instance to the contrary, it must be proved to us that if there were in nature any instances to the contrary, we should have known of them.' This is a sampling/coverage adequacy criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify kinds of uniformities and weigh their dependability
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience must inform us which sorts of uniformities are more to be relied upon; different classes of phenomena yield inductions of differing strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues we need a survey of inductions to ascertain what kinds of uniformities are perfectly invariable and which vary with time, place, or circumstances. E.g., constancy in anatomical structure is more credible than constancy in animal coloration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stronger inductions to test and correct weaker ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger, better-established inductions serve as touchstones against which weaker inductions are tested; incompatible weaker inductions must yield or be revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an induction conflicts with stronger inductions, the weaker one must give way unless the stronger were overstretched. Connecting inductions by ratiocination makes them mutually confirmatory and can raise the weaker to the level of the stronger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek deduction of complex uniformities from simpler laws (parsimony of laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer formulations that reduce complex regularities to the fewest and simplest assumptions (laws) from which the rest follow deductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames the question 'What are the fewest and simplest assumptions, which being granted, the whole existing order of nature would result?' and praises steps like Kepler → Newton where many phenomena were deduced from simpler general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification of deductive consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a complex phenomenon can be deduced from simpler laws, specific empirical verification is still desirable and may be indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Torricellian experiment's result could be deduced from three simpler laws, but verification by specific experience remains desirable and can convert doubtful generalizations into well-established doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between kinds of regularities (simultaneity vs succession; number/geometry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of uniformities (laws of number, space/geometry, causal succession) have different evidential characters and modes of proof; recognize which kind applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes laws of number apply equally to simultaneous and successive phenomena, while geometric laws concern simultaneous phenomena only; this affects how we treat and justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active experimental contrivances to 'unravel the web' of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental rules and contrivances are the techniques for separating intermingled regularities and studying each causal thread independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The metaphor of a web: the regularity in nature is woven of distinct threads, and we must unravel parts of it and exhibit fibres apart. This implies controlled experiments, isolating variables, and designed inquiry rather than passive observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin inductive inquiry from well-established spontaneous generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific investigation pragmatically assumes many obvious uniformities as known (e.g., food nourishes), and builds from them, subject to later revision if limits are found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text defends taking some spontaneous generalizations as starting points rather than adopting a Cartesian blank slate; however, they remain open to ulterior revision as knowledge progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey historical/unscientific inductions to inform scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: A survey of the types of inductions that unscientific practice produces helps identify which uniformities are reliable and hence how to formulate a scientific theory of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The necessary foundation of a scientific formula of induction is a survey of inductions from unscientific practice, to learn what kinds of uniformities have been found invariable versus variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual confirmation via ratiocination increases certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductions that can be connected and deduced from one another through ratiocination are confirmatory and increase the degree of certainty of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inductions confirm each other (one is a conclusion from ratiocination), the conclusion attains at least the certainty of the weakest of those from which it is deduced, and generally all gain in certainty; conversely, incompatible inductions test each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate simple/fundamental laws from derived complex uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific speech, 'laws of nature' ideally denote the simplest independent uniformities; many observed generalizations may be results of these simpler laws and should be recognized as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes three simple laws (example with air weight, fluid pressure propagation, motion from unbalanced pressure) from the derived Torricellian result. Callers to label only the fundamental assumptions as true 'laws of nature'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of induction and that not all inductions reduce to syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some aspects of induction (especially the assumption of uniformity itself) cannot be resolved into prior syllogisms; induction has an ultimate base that is not wholly reducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that while many inductive inferences can be presented as syllogisms, the ultimate universal major (uniformity) includes an instance that cannot be resolved into syllogism; accept a foundational role for certain inductive principles.
